rows.verified: Poorly installed or maintained gas appliances can create fire, explosion, gas-leak and carbon-monoxide hazards.
Employers must comply with relevant gas-safety law to protect workers and members of the public.
In workplaces such as shops, restaurants, schools and hospitals, gas-fitting work must be carried out by a Gas Safe registered engineer qualified for the work.
The employer is responsible for checking that a gas engineer is registered and holds the relevant qualifications.
Gas appliances should be maintained in a safe condition by a competent person and in line with manufacturers' instructions and appropriate standards.
Hospitality and catering employers must keep gas appliances, flues, pipework and safety devices in a safe condition.
Gas-equipment inspection intervals depend on equipment and use, but annual inspection is generally a reasonable minimum unless manufacturer guidance requires otherwise.
Commercial solid-fuel appliances can expose workers and the public to carbon monoxide, requiring effective controls and maintenance.
Gas-safety controls depend on appliance type, fuel, installation, ventilation, flue condition, maintenance history, occupancy and competent-person findings.
Gas-safety evidence is appliance-, premises- and condition-specific and is not an exact parcel-level fire, explosion or poisoning probability.
LPG is flammable and heavier than air, so escaped gas can collect in low areas and create fire, explosion or suffocation hazards.
The LPG user has responsibilities for tank siting, ventilation, tanker access, security, impact protection and emergency arrangements.
A business operating an LPG installation must assess the risks and identify preventive measures under health and safety law.
Where the supplier owns or maintains the storage tank, the site user still needs to coordinate with the supplier to manage installation risks.
Relevant pressure systems must have a written scheme of examination and be examined by a competent person as specified in that scheme.
Users should consider recording pipework routes, risk assessments and maintenance information for the LPG installation.
LPG users should consider workplace structural stability because an escape of gas can lead to fire or explosion.
DSEAR applies to bulk LPG storage, cylinder filling and outdoor cylinder storage areas.
LPG controls depend on fuel quantity, storage type, tank or cylinder condition, ventilation, separation, vehicle impact, pipework, ignition sources and emergency arrangements.
LPG evidence is installation-, inventory- and site-specific and is not an exact parcel-level fire or explosion probability.
